caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000003
attempts.paper_title: Physiological Properties and Behavioral Correlates of Hippocampal Granule Cells and Mossy Cells
attempts.entry_title: Granule cells and mossy cells of the dentate gyrus (Senzai and Buzsaki 2017)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Senzai and Buzsaki (2017) on dandiset 000003, which holds silicon probe recordings of the dentate gyrus and CA3 in 16 mice, in 101 files from 94 recording days, with labelled granule cells, mossy cells, CA3 pyramidal cells and interneurons, sleep states, dentate spikes, light pulses, and positions on a circular T-maze and in open fields. It covers firing by brain state, theta and gamma phase locking, recruitment by dentate spikes, optogenetic tagging, monosynaptic transmission, place fields and remapping, and, on the 17 files that give each unit's shank, depth and the classification of granule and mossy cells.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Senzai and Buzsaki (2017) from dandiset 000003

outcomes.statement: The second-stage classification divided dentate excitatory neurons into 586 putative granule cells (GC) and 500 putative mossy cells (MC).
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells in extracellular recordings, paragraph 2; Figure 1F
outcomes.quote: K-means clustering on the three sets of features reliably segregated excitatory neurons as putative granule cells (n = 586) and putative mossy cells (n = 500)
outcomes.notes: The files hold 609 GC (paper 586, within tolerance) and 568 MC (paper 500, outside the tolerance of 450 to 550), from all 16 mice, counting each of the 101 files once.
deviations: Counts come from the dandiset's labels; the paper's classification was not re-run on all files.

outcomes.statement: Narrow-waveform interneurons have a trough-to-peak latency below 0.425 ms, and among wide-waveform units the excitatory cells have a burst index above the threshold separating them from wide-waveform interneurons.
outcomes.source: Figure 1A; STAR Methods, Unit classification
outcomes.quote: Units with trough-to-peak latency < 0.425 ms were classified as narrow-waveform putative interneurons ... Wide-waveform units were grouped into putative excitatory cells (E cells, red; burst index>1.8) and wide-waveform putative interneurons
outcomes.notes: Under both burst thresholds (1.2 in the Methods, 1.8 in the Figure 1A legend), 98.2% of GC and MC are wide-waveform and bursty and 91.7% or 93.3% of wide-waveform interneurons are wide and not bursty, but 82.5% of narrow-waveform interneurons have a latency below 0.425 ms (40% to 100% by mouse), short of the 90% criterion. The labels pool dentate and CA3 interneurons; 92.7% are below 0.525 ms, the paper's CA3 threshold, and in the 17 files that give the shank 94.4% of the 71 narrow-waveform interneurons on shanks with GC or MC and no CA3 unit are below 0.425 ms (variants). The stored waveforms have their trough at 0.80 ms, so latencies above about 0.75 ms cannot be measured. On the wide-band signal of the 17 files, 64.7% (unfiltered) or 88.5% (300 Hz high-pass) of narrow-waveform interneurons are below 0.425 ms.
deviations: Latency measured on the mean of the first 200 stored waveforms (1.6 ms long, filtering not stated in the files); the paper used unfiltered waveforms.
The Methods and the Figure 1A legend give different burst thresholds (1.2 and 1.8); both were tested.

outcomes.statement: Narrow-waveform interneurons fire faster than wide-waveform interneurons (medians 7.97 and 2.11 Hz; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001).
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells in extracellular recordings, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The mean firing rates of narrow (median = 7.97 Hz) and wide-waveform (median = 2.11 Hz) interneurons were significantly different
outcomes.notes: Narrow-waveform interneurons fire faster than wide-waveform ones (Kruskal-Wallis P = 5.3e-17 over the recording span, 1.4e-15 in awake periods), but the medians are outside tolerance under both readings (5.96 and 2.57 Hz over the recording; 8.75 and 3.08 Hz awake). In the 17 files that give the shank, interneurons on shanks with GC or MC and no CA3 unit have medians of 8.56 and 2.29 Hz over the recording, both within tolerance (P = 3.7e-08); this variant does not decide the outcome.
deviations: The interneuron labels include CA3 interneurons, which the paper counts apart, and the files do not say which region an interneuron is in.
The paper does not define the rate; two readings were tested.

outcomes.statement: The waveform of granule cells is narrower than that of mossy cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells in extracellular recordings, paragraph 3; Figure 1E
outcomes.quote: Overall, the waveform of granule cells was narrower
outcomes.notes: GC median trough-to-peak latency 0.710 ms against MC 0.740 ms (Mann-Whitney P = 2.3e-14). The stored waveforms have their trough at 0.80 ms of 1.6 ms, and 43% of GC and 67% of MC have their peak at the end, so the result partly reflects how often each type is cut off; among units with the peak inside the window GC are not narrower (0.660 against 0.645 ms, P = 0.057). On the wide-band signal of the 17 files (window to 2.4 ms), the unfiltered waveform the Methods use gives GC 0.755 against MC 0.840 ms (P = 0.017); after a 300 Hz high-pass they do not differ (0.710 against 0.720 ms, P = 0.4).
deviations: Measured as trough-to-peak latency on the stored waveforms, where the paper describes the waveform shape through a PCA of its second derivative.

outcomes.statement: In DRD2-Cre::Ai35 mice, 29 of 107 putative mossy cells were suppressed by green light, against none of 202 putative granule cells, 8 of 68 wide-waveform and none of 69 narrow-waveform interneurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Optogenetic validation of the physiology-based separation of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 1H; STAR Methods, Optogenetic tagging
outcomes.quote: 29 out of 107 putative mossy cells were light responsive ... whereas only eight of 68 w-I interneurons and none of the putative granule cells (n = 202) or n-I interneurons (n = 69) were suppressed significantly by green light
outcomes.notes: In 26 DRD2-Cre::Ai35 sessions with 20 ms pulses (4 mice), 68 of 106 MC (0.642) are suppressed by at least 20% with the baseline before the pulse and 71 (0.670) with the baseline later in the cycle, against 6 (0.030) and 13 (0.066) of 198 GC. Wide-waveform interneurons 20 of 88, narrow-waveform 14 of 132. The MC fraction is far above the paper's 29 of 107 and GC are not zero; MC exceed four times the GC fraction under both readings. At a 50% threshold the MC fraction is 0.066. Adding a one-sided Poisson test (P < 0.05) to the 20% rule keeps all 68 MC and 5 GC. The 37 units of the Figure 1H legend equal the 29 MC and 8 wide-waveform interneurons of the text.
deviations: The Methods do not define the baseline of the light-pulse histogram; two readings were tested.
The fifth DRD2 mouse (YutaMouse45) has no 20 ms pulses and is not included.

outcomes.statement: Mossy cells are more active than granule cells during both waking and NREM sleep (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for each).
outcomes.source: Results, Physiological properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: Mossy cells were more active than granule cells during both waking and NREM sleep
outcomes.notes: MC median 0.736 Hz against GC 0.077 Hz in awake periods (Kruskal-Wallis P = 1.8e-114), 0.727 against 0.083 Hz with quiet wake, and 0.913 against 0.391 Hz in NREM (P = 2e-29). With home-cage awake time as wake (a variant), 0.692 against 0.077 Hz (P = 8.1e-102).
deviations: Wake is read as the `awake` periods, or `awake` with `quiet`; the states table does not describe its labels.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells fire most during NREM sleep and at similar rates during wake and REM.
outcomes.source: Results, Physiological properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: Granule cells had their highest firing rates during NREM sleep and similar rates during wake and REM
outcomes.notes: GC fire most in NREM (median 0.391 Hz against 0.077 Hz awake and 0.198 Hz REM; adjusted P 1.3e-86 and 8.7e-31), but REM rates exceed wake rates (adjusted P = 1.4e-25 with awake periods, 6.3e-23 with quiet wake), so wake and REM are not similar by the paper's test. With home-cage awake time as wake (a variant), wake and REM still differ (adjusted P = 3.3e-24).
deviations: The post hoc test is taken as Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney tests; the paper names Kruskal-Wallis only.

outcomes.statement: CA3 pyramidal neurons are most active during wake and least active during REM.
outcomes.source: Results, Physiological properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: CA3 pyramidal neurons were most active during wake and least active during REM
outcomes.notes: CA3 pyramidal cells fire least in REM (0.287 Hz; adjusted P = 1.1e-15 against NREM and 5.4e-09 against wake), but the NREM median (0.459 Hz) is above the wake median (0.441 Hz awake, 0.433 Hz with quiet wake) and the two do not differ (adjusted P = 0.77 and 0.59). The REM part of the claim holds. With home-cage awake time as wake (a variant), the wake median is 0.412 Hz and NREM against wake gives adjusted P = 0.14; CA3 units fire at similar rates awake in the home cage and during behaviour (0.424 and 0.415 Hz).
deviations: The paper's CA3 units come from a separate classification (Figure S2); here the dandiset's `pyramidal cell` label is used.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells increase their firing in NREM sleep compared with waking, while mossy cells fire at equivalent rates in the two states.
outcomes.source: Figure 1D; Discussion, first paragraph
outcomes.quote: Granule cells had cell bodies located near the depth of DS2 reversal, had increased firing in NREM compared to waking ... In contrast, mossy cells ... had equivalent firing rates in NREM and waking
outcomes.notes: Median NREM to wake ratio 4.63 for GC and 1.11 for MC (Mann-Whitney P = 3.9e-141; 4.28 and 1.11 with quiet wake), and the GC ratio is above the MC ratio in every mouse with both. The part saying MC fire at equivalent rates does not fully hold, as MC NREM rates are slightly above wake rates (Wilcoxon P = 1.4e-06). With home-cage awake time, 4.56 and 1.10.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by theta oscillations than mossy cells and fire at later theta phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
outcomes.source: Results, Physiological properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: Granule cells fired on earlier phases of gamma waves ... and later phases of theta oscillations ... Granule cells were more strongly phase-modulated by both gamma ... and theta
outcomes.notes: Modulated units 483 GC and 532 MC. Theta MRL GC 0.422 against MC 0.339 (Kruskal-Wallis P = 1.5e-20); GC fire later (circular means 30.8 and 12.0 degrees from the peak; P = 1e-17 with phases on (-pi, pi], 0.82 on [0, 2 pi)). After subtracting the uniform-phase expectation for the spike count (GC have fewer spikes), GC are still higher, at P = 0.00056. The bias-corrected MRL comparison (P = 0.00056) does not reach the paper's P < 0.0001. In the 17 files where it can be checked the theta-reference channel has a positive DS2 (+459 to +786 uV), so it lies below the DS2 reversal.
deviations: Phases from the theta-reference channel the conversion flagged, during up to an hour of awake periods per file; the paper's periods and reference channel are not stated.
Phase comparisons depend on where the cycle is cut; both cuts are shown and the claim holds on one.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by gamma oscillations than mossy cells and fire at earlier gamma phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
outcomes.source: Results, Physiological properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: Granule cells fired on earlier phases of gamma waves ... Granule cells were more strongly phase-modulated by both gamma
outcomes.notes: Modulated units 345 GC and 475 MC. Gamma MRL GC 0.319 against MC 0.212 (P = 4.8e-43; 0.219 against 0.166, P = 4.1e-18, after subtracting the uniform-phase expectation); GC fire earlier (circular means -20.2 and 1.7 degrees; P = 1.2e-23 on (-pi, pi], 0.18 on [0, 2 pi)).
deviations: As theta-modulation.

outcomes.statement: Slow-firing neurons are more strongly coupled to gamma than fast-firing ones (GC r = -0.176, MC r = -0.184, P < 0.0001 for each).
outcomes.source: Results, Physiological properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, slow firing neurons had stronger phase coupling to gamma waves than fast firing cells
outcomes.notes: Over all units with a gamma MRL, GC r = -0.177 (P = 3.6e-05, within tolerance) and MC r = -0.161 (P = 0.00013, just outside the tolerance and above P = 0.0001). Over modulated units, GC -0.397 and MC -0.253, both P below 0.0001 and outside tolerance.
deviations: The paper does not say which units or which rate the correlation uses; two unit sets were tested with the rate over the recording span.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells are more effectively recruited by type 2 dentate spikes than mossy cells and fire earlier (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
outcomes.source: Results, Physiological properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2; Figure 2D and 2E
outcomes.quote: Granule cells were also more effectively recruited to LFP DS2 than mossy cells ... and fired earlier
outcomes.notes: Median DS2 peak ratio GC 6.88 against MC 4.82 (Kruskal-Wallis P = 1.1e-10); median peak time -3.0 against +1.0 ms (P = 2.2e-09). 10 GC and 14 MC dropped for a zero baseline.
deviations: The DS2 events are those stored in the files; the peak-ratio baseline (50 to 100 ms on both sides) is a choice, as the paper does not give it.

outcomes.statement: 5.5% of granule cells monosynaptically excite mossy cells (32 pairs), whereas no mossy cell significantly excites a granule cell.
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission, paragraph 1; Figure 3B and 3C
outcomes.quote: The spike transmission probability between excitatory neuron pairs determined that 5.5% of the granule cells monosynaptically excited mossy cells (n = 32 pairs), whereas no mossy cell significantly excited putative granule cells
outcomes.notes: Among 4713 GC-MC pairs the automatic test finds 65 GC to MC pairs and 8 MC to GC pairs. The fraction is 0.107 (pairs over GC), 0.0805 (GC with a target over GC) or 0.0138 (pairs over tested pairs), none within 0.0495 to 0.0605. GC to MC pairs outnumber MC to GC pairs 65 to 8. Stricter thresholds lower both counts (56 and 6 at the 99.99999th percentile). For 22 GC to MC pairs the largest bin is the first of the window (1.5 to 2 ms); without them 43 pairs remain (0.0706 of GC). Of the 8 MC to GC pairs, 6 are in YutaMouse33, 4 involve one GC (unit 3 of YutaMouse33-150224) that is also synchronous with each of those MC, and 5 are also detected as GC to MC pairs, which fits common input. In the 17 files that give the shank, 17 of 39 GC to MC pairs are on one shank.
deviations: The paper inspected and refined each detection by hand; the automatic test alone is used here.
The fraction 5.5% can be read three ways; all are shown.

outcomes.statement: Spike transmission probability from granule cells to mossy cells increases from the first to the second spike of a granule cell burst (P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission, paragraph 2; Figure 3E to 3G
outcomes.quote: Spike transmission probability increased from first to second spike
outcomes.notes: For the 65 detected pairs, the median transmission probability is 0.0066 for first and 0.0334 for second burst spikes, higher in 58 pairs (Wilcoxon P = 1.2e-09); it holds with bursts at 4 ms (P = 4.4e-08) and 10 ms (P = 5.5e-10). The detected pairs are partly reproduced (see monosyn-gc-to-mc) and number 65 against the paper's 32. It also holds with only burst intervals of 3.5 to 6 ms, where the two response windows do not overlap (58 of 65, P = 7.6e-10), with a baseline hollowed by 60% (P = 1.2e-09), and without the 22 first-bin pairs (41 of 43, P = 3.8e-11). First spikes transmit less than single spikes (0.0066 against 0.0147), which the outputs do not explain.
deviations: Bursts are spikes at most 6 ms apart, a choice; the paper does not define them.
Transmission is the excess over the plain Gaussian baseline of the Methods.

outcomes.statement: GC to MC spike transmission is lower during NREM sleep than during waking (n = 31, P < 0.005).
outcomes.source: Results, State-dependent changes in spike transmission probabilities, paragraph 1; Figure 4B
outcomes.quote: Granule cell to mossy cell and granule cell to interneuron comparisons showed reduced probability of spike transmission during NREM compared to wake
outcomes.notes: For 65 detected pairs, median transmission 0.0125 from GC spikes in awake periods and 0.0108 in NREM, lower in NREM for 34 pairs; Wilcoxon P = 0.39. The pairs are the automatic detections (see monosyn-gc-to-mc), not the paper's 31. Without the 22 first-bin pairs NREM is lower in 24 of 43 (P = 0.27); in the 17 files that give the shank, in 20 of 39 (P = 0.86).
deviations: Uses the automatic pair detections in place of the paper's curated pairs.

outcomes.statement: Synchronous co-activation within 1 ms is found in 23% of mossy cells and 9% of CA3 pyramidal cells, but in fewer than 0.2% of granule cell pairs.
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Only <0.2% of granule cell pairs showed significant peaks at < 1 ms while 23% of mossy cells and 9% of CA3 pyramidal cells showed synchronous (< 1 ms) co-activation
outcomes.notes: GC pairs 4 of 3155 (0.0013, within the claim). MC 0.0766 of pairs or 0.433 of cells; CA3 0.0120 of pairs or 0.102 of cells; none within the tolerance of 0.23 and 0.09. Read as cells, MC and CA3 exceed the GC pair fraction more than ten times. In the 17 files that give the shank no synchronous pair is on one shank (0 of 160 MC, 0 of 51 CA3), so leaving out same-shank pairs changes little (cells MC 0.494, CA3 0.267 there); 143 of 160 synchronous MC pairs are on neighbouring shanks. No synchronous pair shares more than 15% of the sparser unit's spikes within 0.5 ms (MC at most 5.8%), so none looks like one neuron sorted twice.
deviations: Automatic detections without the paper's manual refinement.
Pairs recorded on one shank cannot be left out in 83 of 101 files, which do not give the shank; in the other 17 files none of the synchronous pairs is on one shank.

outcomes.statement: On the circular T-maze, the fraction of active neurons (above 1 Hz) is higher in the central arm than in the side arms, for granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001 for each).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 5B
outcomes.quote: The fraction of active neurons (> 1 Hz) was significantly higher in the central arm compared to the side arms
outcomes.notes: The central-arm median fraction of active units is above the side-arm median for GC (0.020 against 0.018, P = 0.043), MC (0.314 against 0.272, P = 2.2e-06) and CA3 (0.214 against 0.189, P = 0.048); only MC reach P < 0.00001. The bin-wise test treats smoothed, neighbouring bins as independent; compared unit by unit (a variant) the central arm is more active for MC (P = 2.8e-05) but not for GC (higher in 17, lower in 31 of 253 units, P = 0.83) or CA3 (P = 0.21).
deviations: T-maze runs are taken from the start of the central arm to 10 cm before the reward port in trials without light; the paper uses the time from gate opening to arrival at the reward.
The meaning of the linearised T-maze positions is inferred from the values and the maze dimensions.

outcomes.statement: Few granule cells have two or more place fields on the T-maze (6.6%), against 57.8% of mossy cells and 36.1% of CA3 pyramidal cells (Kolmogorov-Smirnov P < 0.0001).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 5C and 5D
outcomes.quote: only a small fraction (6.6% of recorded cells) had two or more. In contrast, 57.8% of mossy cells and 36.1% of CA3 pyramidal neurons had two or more place fields
outcomes.notes: Of all units, 4.3% of GC (253), 63.7% of MC (303) and 43.1% of CA3 (341) have two or more fields; of units with a field, 24.4%, 78.1% and 66.8%. No reading puts all three in tolerance (MC misses by 0.001 under reading a). GC have the fewest fields (KS P = 3.2e-53 against MC). The units come from 7 mice; the paper reports 213, 225 and 249 units from 9 mice.
deviations: Fields are counted on a map of the central arm from all runs plus each side arm, smoothed per segment; the paper builds left and right choice maps without saying how fields are combined.
The 'local maximum' of the field rule is taken iteratively from the highest unassigned bin.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells have the lowest within-field peak firing rates (GC against MC, Kolmogorov-Smirnov P < 0.003) and the lowest spatial information of the three types (P < 0.0005).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 5E and 5F
outcomes.quote: Of the three neuron types, granule cells had the lowest within-place field peak firing rates ... and lowest spatial information

statistics.about: within-field peak rate, GC against MC

outcomes.notes: Within-field peak GC 2.63 Hz against MC 5.68 Hz (KS P = 4.5e-05); spatial information GC 0.035 bits/s against MC 0.603 (P = 1.6e-49) and CA3 0.293 (P = 1.5e-29).
deviations: As tmaze-multiple-fields.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of splitter cells, whose central-arm firing predicts the coming turn, is comparable in granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The fraction of splitter cells was comparable in the three principal cell groups
outcomes.notes: Splitters 0 of 17 GC, 4 of 179 MC and 4 of 141 CA3 with a central-arm field; chi-square P = 0.76. Fisher's exact test gives P = 1 for GC against MC and against CA3 and 0.73 for MC against CA3. Under equal fractions 0.40 GC splitters would be expected, so the GC comparison has almost no power.
deviations: The paper names no test for comparing the fractions; a chi-square test was fixed in the criterion.

outcomes.statement: For neurons with stable place fields, the remapping index between open fields A and B is above zero in each group (Wilcoxon signed-rank; GC P < 0.05, MC and CA3 P < 0.00001).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2; Figure 6C and 6D
outcomes.quote: For neurons with significant place fields ... the remapping index was significantly higher than zero in each group
outcomes.notes: Place cells GC 27, MC 116, CA3 145 (paper 30, 111, 144), of which 27, 116 and 143 have a remapping index; median remapping index 0.128 (P = 0.0013), 0.293 (P = 1.5e-13) and 0.207 (P = 8.6e-14). Units per type 246, 182 and 317 in 5 mice (paper 247, 181, 317 in 5 mice).
deviations: The place-field 'local maximum' is the map's peak; the speed is from positions smoothed over 0.25 s.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells with stable place fields remap less than mossy cells (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.034; post hoc GC against MC P = 0.028).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2; Figure 6D
outcomes.quote: but granule cells showed less remapping compared to mossy cells
outcomes.notes: The GC median index (0.128) is below the MC median (0.293) but neither test is significant (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.306; GC against MC P = 0.114, 0.342 after Bonferroni). With the variant place-cell rule, GC against MC P = 0.0648.
deviations: The paper's post hoc test is not named; Bonferroni-corrected Mann-Whitney tests are used.

outcomes.statement: Only 36.7% of granule cells with place fields (11 of 30) remap, against 61.3% of mossy cells (68 of 111) and 55.6% of CA3 pyramidal cells (80 of 144).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2; Figure 6C
outcomes.quote: only a minority of granule cells (36.7%, n = 11 out of n = 30 place cells) showed remapping, whereas the majority of both mossy cells (61.3%, n=68 out of n = 111 place cells) and CA3 pyramidal neurons (55.6%, n = 80 out of n = 144) did
outcomes.notes: 11 of 27 GC (0.407), 65 of 116 MC (0.560) and 73 of 143 CA3 (0.510) place cells remap. MC and CA3 are within tolerance; GC is 0.003 above it. GC remap least at every threshold shown (0.1 to 0.3).

outcomes.statement: Population-vector remapping is smaller for granule cells than for mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells, for populations of 5, 10, 15 and 20 place cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatial and memory properties of granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 3; Figure 6E to 6G
outcomes.quote: The magnitude of population remapping was significantly smaller for granule cells compared to mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells ... These results remained robust within a range of threshold values with different numbers of neurons comprising the population vector
outcomes.notes: For 5, 10, 15 and 20 cells, the GC median index (0.162 to 0.210) is below the MC (0.253 to 0.302) and CA3 (0.251 to 0.352) medians, Kruskal-Wallis P from 5.8e-35 to 8.1e-190. 71% to 89% of GC draws fall below the MC median. These P values treat 1000 overlapping draws from the same 27 GC as independent and do not measure the evidence. With all place cells together the index is 0.22 for GC and 0.25 for MC, and permuting the GC and MC labels gives P = 0.32 for that difference.
deviations: Place cells pooled across sessions and mice for the draws; the paper does not say whether it pooled.

outcomes.statement: Mossy cells rarely inherit place fields from single presynaptic granule cells; of 10 place fields of connected granule cells, only 2 overlapped a field of the postsynaptic mossy cell.
outcomes.source: Results, Transmission of place information between granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 1; Figure 7A and 7B
outcomes.quote: Across 10 place fields from granule cells and 48 place fields from mossy cells, only two place fields showed overlap between monosynaptically connected pairs
outcomes.notes: 5 of 16 GC fields (0.31) of GC with a detected MC partner overlap a partner MC field, within the criterion of at most a third; 15 of 23 GC partners have no T-maze field (paper 11 of 18). The result is close to the criterion's limit and uses the automatic pair detections (see monosyn-gc-to-mc). With the partner replaced by a random other MC of the session (1000 draws), the overlap is 0.38 (5th to 95th percentile 0.19 to 0.62) and 33% of draws are at or below 0.31, so the overlap with the connected MC is at the chance level.
deviations: "Rarely" was fixed as at most a third of GC fields; the paper gives 2 of 10.
Pairs are automatic detections, not the paper's curated pairs.

outcomes.statement: In the open fields, the rate maps of connected granule cells and mossy cells are not correlated within the granule cell's place field (median near 0, n = 19, Wilcoxon P = 0.60).
outcomes.source: Results, Transmission of place information between granule cells and mossy cells, paragraph 2; Figure 7J
outcomes.quote: GC-MC map correlations of all comparisons in which the presynaptic GC had significant place fields. Note median correlation around 0
outcomes.notes: 18 comparisons from 6 pairs in 4 sessions; median r = -0.038, Wilcoxon P = 0.67; 5 of 18 above 0.5 (paper 2 of 19). The 18 comparisons come from only 6 pairs, so they are not independent.
deviations: Pairs are automatic detections; the open-field sessions include the curtain sessions, as the paper's five sessions per pair do.

outcomes.statement: Mossy cells are located deeper than granule cells relative to the reversal of the type 2 dentate spike (DS2) (Mann-Whitney P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Figure 1G; Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells in extracellular recordings, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: MC were located significantly deeper than GC
outcomes.notes: In the 17 files with the wide-band signal and shanks (4 mice; 139 GC, 226 MC with at least 20 spikes in the wide-band window), the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, read from the wide-band signal, has a median of +580 uV for MC and +232 uV for GC (Mann-Whitney P = 2e-40); 100% of MC (to two decimals) and 80% of GC sit where DS2 is positive, and MC are deeper in each of the 4 mice. With the site the electrodes table gives (a variant), +271 against -38 uV (P = 5.7e-09), with YutaMouse33 reversed; the two sites share the LFP column for 9% of units and the DS2 sign for 63%.
deviations: Depth is read from the DS2 amplitude at the site, as the files give no site coordinates; the paper measures distance from the DS2 reversal.

17 of 101 files only. The site is the wide-band column where the unit's spike is largest (300 Hz high-pass, about 150 s of signal per file), as the electrodes table's channel map disagrees with the wide-band signal; the criterion's shank channel taken through the table is shown as a variant.
DS2 amplitude from about 220 s of LFP per file (the two LFP chunks with the most DS2 peaks).

outcomes.statement: K-means clustering on the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, the NREM to wake rate ratio and two principal components of the waveform's second derivative separates excitatory dentate units into granule cells and mossy cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells in extracellular recordings, paragraph 2; Figure 1D to 1F; STAR Methods, Unit classification
outcomes.quote: Based on the bimodality of the distribution, K-means clustering over the four parameters was performed to classify E units into putative GC (yellow) and MC (magenta)
outcomes.notes: On 364 GC and MC of the 17 files (32 dropped for fewer than 20 spikes in the wide-band window, no DS2 site or a zero awake rate), k-means on the DS2 amplitude at the wide-band site, the Methods' NREM to wake ratio and two components of the second derivative of the unfiltered wide-band waveform agrees with the labels for 95.3% of units (93% to 97% by mouse). Without the DS2 amplitude 89.0%, without the first waveform component 88.5%, without the ratio 94.2%. With the log ratio 95.6%, with home-cage awake time 94.8%, with the stored waveforms and the table's site 92.8%.
deviations: Run on 17 of 101 files (364 of 1177 GC and MC); the paper ran it on all excitatory units.
The site and the waveform are read from the wide-band signal (about 150 s per file), as the electrodes table's channel map disagrees with it; the stored waveforms with the table's site are a variant.
Wake is the `awake` periods, as fixed in the criterion; the Methods name awake time in the home cage, shown as a variant.
The four features are standardised and clustered directly; the paper took a second PCA before k-means, which does not change k-means on all components.
The second-derivative window starts at the trough; the Methods say 0 to 0.8 ms without naming the origin.

outcomes.statement: Granule cells reside 59 +- 35 um above the mossy cells they drive.
outcomes.source: Results, Granule cell-mossy cell spike transmission, paragraph 1; Figure 3D
outcomes.quote: Granule cells resided 59±35 μm above their driven mossy cell partners
outcomes.notes: Needs the positions of the recording sites in um. The electrodes tables give x, y and z as NaN in every file, the order of sites along a shank is not stated, and 83 of 101 files do not say which shank a unit was on. The paper's own monosynaptic pairs were not converted either. The Methods give 8 sites per shank on the 8-shank probes and 10 on the 6-shank probes, staggered with 20 um vertical separation, but the table's site numbers do not follow depth (the DS2 profile along them crosses zero more than once on 43 of 64 shanks with a crossing), and a unit's largest wide-band column lies on the shank the table gives for only 45% of units. In the 17 files that give the shank, the order of each shank's stored waveform channels can be recovered from the units' spikes in the wide-band signal, and along it the DS2 profile crosses zero once on 43 of the 51 shanks that cross, so it is consistent with depth. This attempt wrote no criterion for the claim and ran no test on that order; a new attempt could test it on these 17 files (39 detected GC to MC pairs).

outcomes.statement: Granule cell spikes show a delay from the soma to the proximal dendrites, absent in mossy cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Identification of granule cells and mossy cells in extracellular recordings, paragraph 3; Figure S3D to S3F
outcomes.quote: Indeed, the spikes of granule cells showed a delay from the soma to the proximal dendrites ... whereas no such delays were observed in putative mossy cells
outcomes.notes: Needs each unit's waveform along the shank with the sites' vertical positions; the files give no site coordinates (x, y, z are NaN) and the stored waveforms span 1.6 ms at the channels of the shank without their positions. In 83 files the shank itself is not given. The wide-band signal gives each unit's spike on every column, and in those 17 files the order of each shank's stored channels, recovered from the units' spikes, is consistent with depth (see gc-mc-distance). This attempt wrote no criterion for the claim and ran no test of a delay along that order; a new attempt could.

findings.statement: In 24 files the end index of the first unit in the units table is short by a multiple of 65,536 spikes (k = 1 to 7). The missing spikes open the second unit's spike train, which then restarts at the beginning of the recording, so the second unit's times are not sorted. The first moved spike follows the first unit's last stored spike by 2 ms to 0.5 s. This looks like an integer overflow at conversion; the waveforms follow the same boundaries.
The genotypes in the files (6 SST-Cre, 5 Drd2-Cre::Ai35, 4 POMC-Cre::Arch, 1 POMC-Cre::Ai35) do not match the paper's 16 mice (7 SST-Cre, 5 DRD2-Cre::Ai35, 3 POMC-Cre::Ai35 and 1 wild type).

83 of 101 files do not say which shank each unit was recorded on (`shank_id` is a cluster number, and there is no `electrode_group`), and no file gives site coordinates (x, y, z are NaN). The paper's depth measures can be computed for 17 files only, and distances between cells not at all.

The T-maze position series (`twhl_linearized`, `twhl_norm`) are not described. The values show column 0 of `twhl_linearized` runs along the central arm (0 to 2) and column 1 is an angle along the circular side arms, negative for the left arm, which fits the maze in the Methods but is not stated.
The states table holds `awake`, `quiet`, `nrem`, `rem` and `transit` without a description; the paper names wake, NREM and REM, and whether `quiet` counts as wake is not stated.

The interneuron labels (narrow-waveform, wide-waveform) do not say whether the unit is in the dentate gyrus or CA3, which the paper separates; only the excitatory label was split by region (granule cell or CA3 pyramidal cell).

The monosynaptic connections the authors detected and curated (`MonoSynConvClick.mat`) were not converted (the conversion code comments them out), so the pair-based results (Figures 3, 4 and 7) cannot be checked on the authors' pairs.
The dandiset holds 568 mossy cells and 609 granule cells against the paper's 500 and 586, and 237 units labelled `missing` (units of the spike sorting with no row in the authors' unit summary).
The light-pulse series PulseStim_5V_20ms_LD12 of YutaMouse57-161006 holds 89,086 times of which 24,286 are duplicates, and its times decrease once.

The units table has two layouts. 18 files (mice 33, 41, 42 and 54) carry an `electrode_group` column naming each unit's shank, one of them without waveforms (YutaMouse33-150218, which the conversion script lists as excluded); the other 83 files do not.

Seven dates hold two files of one mouse (the second named with `b`). They share no spike trains, so they are different recordings, but the metadata do not say whether they come from a second probe or a second session.
The Methods give a burst index threshold of 1.2 for excitatory cells, and the Figure 1A legend gives 1.8.

In the 17 files with the wide-band signal and each unit's shank, the electrodes table's assignment of columns to shanks and sites disagrees with the data. The column where a unit's spike is largest in the wide-band signal lies on the shank the units table gives for 45% of units (11% to 79% by file) and is the table's own site for 9%, and the DS2 amplitude along the table's site numbers crosses zero more than once on 43 of 64 shanks where it crosses at all. The wide-band and LFP columns match each other. The units' shanks (`electrode_group`) and stored waveform channels fit the wide-band signal under one fixed map of columns, the same in all 4 mice (a map from three mice gives the column of a unit's largest spike for 78% to 89% of units in the fourth, against 5% to 13% for the table), so the error is in the table, whose blocks of 8 rows do not match the probe's columns.

The stored spike waveforms are about 5 times larger than the same spikes in the wide-band signal (median peak-to-peak 421 against 81 uV, 300 Hz high-pass), and their filtering and scaling are not described. They match the wide-band spike best after a 300 Hz high-pass (median correlation 0.987, against 0.981 unfiltered and 0.867 at 800 Hz), with a gain of 5.08, close to 5.13, the inverse of the wide-band conversion of 0.195 uV per count, which is consistent with waveforms stored in ADC counts and read as microvolts. Each holds 1.6 ms with the trough at 0.8 ms, which cuts off the peak of 43% of GC, 67% of MC and 78% of CA3 waveforms.

entries.name: 000003-senzai-2017
entries.title: Granule cells and mossy cells of the dentate gyrus (Senzai and Buzsaki 2017)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Senzai and Buzsaki (2017) on dandiset 000003, which holds silicon probe recordings of the dentate gyrus and CA3 in 16 mice, in 101 files from 94 recording days, with labelled granule cells, mossy cells, CA3 pyramidal cells and interneurons, sleep states, dentate spikes, light pulses, and positions on a circular T-maze and in open fields. It covers firing by brain state, theta and gamma phase locking, recruitment by dentate spikes, optogenetic tagging, monosynaptic transmission, place fields and remapping, and, on the 17 files that give each unit's shank, depth and the classification of granule and mossy cells.
